introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION A: COMPOSITION (20 MARKS)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: definition and the 'good servant, dangerous master' idea.
2. Benefits: communication and trade (mobile money).
3. Benefits: education, health, agriculture.
4. Dangers: addiction, false information, crime.
5. Dangers: unemployment and pollution.
6. The way forward: responsible use by parents, government and companies; conclusion.

**Model composition (529 words)**

Technology is the application of scientific knowledge to solve practical problems, and today it touches almost every part of our lives. From the mobile phone in a farmer's pocket to the computer in a hospital laboratory, it has changed how we work, learn, trade and even think. However, like fire, it is a good servant but a dangerous master, and a wise society must understand both its gifts and its risks.

The first and most obvious benefit is communication. A student in Buea can now send a message to a relative in Canada in seconds, and a trader in Douala can follow the price of cocoa on the world market. Mobile money services allow a rural woman to pay school fees or receive a payment without travelling for hours to a bank. In this way, technology has shortened distances and brought opportunities to people who were once isolated.

Technology has also transformed education and health. With the internet, a learner may watch a lesson on photosynthesis, read a library book or follow a course offered by a foreign university. In hospitals, scanners and laboratory machines help doctors to diagnose diseases early, and in some remote areas a nurse can consult a specialist by telephone. In agriculture, improved seeds, irrigation pumps and weather information have increased yields and reduced losses for many farmers.

Nevertheless, the same inventions bring serious problems. Many young people spend long hours on social media and video games, neglecting their studies, their family and their health. Moreover, false information spreads on the internet faster than the truth, and it can destroy reputations or provoke hatred and violence. Criminals also use technology to steal money, to threaten others or to deceive the innocent through fake messages.

Another danger concerns employment. Machines can do in an hour what a team of workers did in a day, so factories and offices may reduce their staff. Unless workers are trained in new skills, unemployment may increase, especially in developing countries where technical education is weak. Technology can also damage the environment, because discarded phones, batteries and computers poison the soil and water when they are not recycled properly.

It would therefore be foolish either to reject technology completely or to accept it without thought. The solution lies in responsible use. Parents and teachers should guide children in choosing useful content and in limiting the time they spend online. Governments should pass and enforce laws against cybercrime, protect personal data and invest in digital education so that every child, in town or village, can benefit. Companies should be encouraged to recycle old equipment and to create new jobs rather than only to replace workers.

In conclusion, technology is neither a blessing nor a curse in itself. Its value depends on the intentions and the discipline of those who use it. If we use it to learn, to heal, to produce and to unite people, it will build a better world. If we use it carelessly, it will waste our time, weaken our values and widen the gap between the rich and the poor. The challenge of our generation is to master technology so that it serves humanity, and not humanity technology.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Listing only the advantages (or only the dangers) of 'Technology' without a clear line of argument: an open one-word topic needs a thesis.
